title: Fate and Ragnarök
subtitle: An ending built into the world

learningObjectives.text: Identify the main idea in Fate and Ragnarök.
Keep the claim attached to its cited source and source type.

ref-source.work: The Younger Edda; Also called Snorre's Edda, or The Prose Edda
ref-source.author: Snorri Sturluson
ref-source.excerpt: es of the gods, of the giants and of men are swallowed up by the sea, and the end has come. This is Ragnarok, the twilight of the gods. But the radiant dawn follows the night. The earth, completely green, rises again from the sea, and where the mews have but just been rocking on restless waves, rich fields unplowed and unsown, now wave their golden harvests

ref-secondary.author: Anonymous Old Norse poets
ref-secondary.excerpt: l. Doom of the gods: the phrase “ragna rök” has been rather unfortunately Anglicized into the word “ragnarok” (the Norse term is not a proper name), and rök, “doom,” has been confused with rökkr, “darkness,” and so translated “dusk of the Gods,” or “Götterdämmerung.” 40. In the manuscript most of this stanza is abbreviated to the first letters of the words.

narrativeBlocks.title: Fate and Ragnarök
narrativeBlocks.body: Ragnarök gives Norse myth a tragic horizon: even gods move toward a known catastrophe rather than escaping consequence.

narrativeBlocks.title: Source boundary
narrativeBlocks.body: This starter lesson uses the local scaffold source while deeper primary passages and scholarly comparisons are added. Keep the source’s genre and date in view.

narrativeBlocks.title: What the second source adds
narrativeBlocks.body: The additional corpus record gives a second lens on the same tradition. Compare it with the first source instead of treating either as a complete canon.

narrativeBlocks.title: How to read this evidence
narrativeBlocks.body: Ask what kind of source this is, who translated or organized it, what it can actually prove, and whether another text preserves a different version.

narrativeBlocks.title: The cross-pantheon hook
narrativeBlocks.body: Notice what this tradition emphasizes differently: the same broad theme can carry a very different moral and cultural pressure.
